Problem: _site/ kept showing up as untracked in git.
What caused it: Quarto rebuilds the site into _site/ every time I render.

What I learned: Check the file path at the top of the tab before editing, since every post’s file is called index.qmd.

What caused it: The YAML says bibliography: references.bib but the file didn’t exist yet.
How I fixed it: Created references.bib in the post folder and pasted the BibTeX from the journal’s download link.

title: Footnotes Unfolded
text:
The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck


What climate science can and can’t tell you about the fire weather outside your door








Oct 12, 2026


Anali Nanayakkara












Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?


22,500 forecasts, 24 commodities, and one question about the weather


I checked every ABARES farm forecast since 2000 against what actually happened. The answer depends on which one you’re holding.





Jun 14, 2026


Anali Nanayakkara





No matching items

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
text:
If you live anywhere near the bush in southeastern Australia, you probably remember where you were in the summer of 2019/20. The fires burned at least 19.4 million hectares, destroyed around 5,900 buildings and killed at least 34 people. Smoke reached cities hundreds of kilometres from any fire front, and nearly 80% of Australians said they were affected in some way (Oldenborgh et al. 2021). The damage didn’t stop at the fire front. A Monash study found hospital visits for breathing problems in NSW were 6% higher that season than in the two seasons before, and 45% higher in the New England and North West region (Wen et al. 2022).
So the question most people asked afterwards was a simple one: was that a freak season, or is it going to keep happening? Put another way, did climate change make it more likely?
That’s harder to answer than it sounds. Bushfires have always been part of living in Australia, and no study can point at a single fire and say “climate change caused this one”. What scientists can do is ask a narrower question: have the weather conditions that make fires like this possible become more common? That’s the question an international team led by Geert Jan van Oldenborgh set out to answer, and their findings are what this post walks through.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
text:
If you live anywhere near the bush in southeastern Australia, you probably remember where you were in the summer of 2019/20. The fires burned at least 19.4 million hectares, destroyed around 5,900 buildings and killed at least 34 people. Smoke reached cities hundreds of kilometres from any fire front, and nearly 80% of Australians said they were affected in some way (Oldenborgh et al. 2021). The damage didn’t stop at the fire front. A Monash study found hospital visits for breathing problems in NSW were 6% higher that season than in the two seasons before, and 45% higher in the New England and North West region (Wen et al. 2022).
So the question most people asked afterwards was a simple one: was that a freak season, or is it going to keep happening? Put another way, did climate change make it more likely?
That’s harder to answer than it sounds. Bushfires have always been part of living in Australia, and no study can point at a single fire and say “climate change caused this one”. What scientists can do is ask a narrower question: have the weather conditions that make fires like this possible become more common? That’s the question an international team led by Geert Jan van Oldenborgh set out to answer, and their findings are what this post walks through.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
text:
Measuring “fire weather”
To compare seasons fairly, you need one number that sums up how dangerous the weather is for fire. The researchers used the Fire Weather Index, a scale that combines four ingredients you’d recognise from any hot, windy day on a total fire ban: temperature, humidity, wind and recent rainfall. The higher the index, the more easily a fire starts and the faster it spreads.
It’s a good stand-in for the real thing. In this region, seasons with a high Fire Weather Index tend to be the seasons where the most land burns, especially from November to February (Oldenborgh et al. 2021). And on that index, 2019/20 was the worst season since detailed records began in 1979.
With a way to measure fire weather sorted, the next step was working out how often a season like that should happen, now compared with a century ago.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
text:
Where the evidence comes from
The study looked at the coastal strip between the Great Dividing Range and the sea, from roughly northern NSW down through eastern Victoria, which is where the damage was worst. It drew on three sources of evidence:

Weather records. A detailed reconstruction of the atmosphere called ERA5, covering 1979 to January 2020, plus Bureau of Meteorology station records going back to 1910 for temperature and 1900 for rainfall.
Climate models. Large sets of computer simulations of the climate, run both with and without the warming humans have added. Four of them were used to calculate the Fire Weather Index.
A comparison between two worlds. By comparing the simulated climate of around 1900 with today’s, the researchers could estimate how much more likely a season like Black Summer has become.

The models and the records don’t fully agree, and that disagreement turns out to be one of the most important parts of the story.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
section: So, has it become more likely?
text:
So, has it become more likely?
Yes. Figure 1 shows the main result. The climate models say fire weather as extreme as 2019/20 is at least 30% more likely than it was in the early 1900s, with a best estimate of around 80%. The actual weather records suggest a far bigger jump, at least four times as likely, although the authors think that figure is probably inflated because the record only starts in 1979.








Figure 1: Every estimate says fire weather like Black Summer is more likely than it was in the early 1900s. Bars show the smallest increase each source can confidently support, and dots show the best estimate where one exists. The weather records have no upper limit, so there is no dot for that row. Values from Oldenborgh et al. (2021).





Why such a gap between the models and the records? The models are known to underestimate how fast heatwaves have been getting hotter. Because heat is the biggest driver of the increase (more on that next), that weakness drags their answer down. So the 30% figure is best read as a floor, not a forecast. The true increase is probably higher. It’s just the most the researchers could defend with the tools they had.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
section: It’s the heat, not (only) the drought
text:
It’s the heat, not (only) the drought
If fire weather has got worse, the obvious next question is which ingredient changed. Table 1 breaks it down.




Table 1: Heat is the ingredient that climate change has pushed hardest. Rainfall, the one most people blame, shows no long-term change the study could link to warming.






Ingredient
Why it matters for fire
What changed since the early 1900s




Heat
Dries out leaves, grass and bark so they catch and burn faster
The biggest single driver in most models. A heatwave like December 2019 is at least twice as likely, and weather records suggest about ten times


Humidity
Dry air pulls moisture out of fuel
Drier air added to the risk, and was the main driver in one of the four models


Wind
Pushes a fire forward and carries embers ahead of it
A smaller part of the increase, and it mattered more in some models than others


Rainfall
Wet fuel is hard to ignite
No long-term trend linked to warming. The 2019 drought was real, but more than half of it came from two natural climate patterns








This is the part that surprises people. Drought is what most of us link with Black Summer, and 2019 really was Australia’s driest year on record. But when the researchers looked for a long-term drying trend caused by climate change, they couldn’t find one. More than half of the rainfall shortfall from July to December 2019 came from two natural climate patterns in the oceans and atmosphere around Australia, which happened to line up badly that year (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).
That doesn’t prove climate change had no effect on rainfall. It means the study couldn’t detect one. What it could detect, clearly, was heat: a heatwave like the one in December 2019 would have been one to two degrees cooler in the climate of 1900.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
section: What this means if you live near the bush
text:
What this means if you live near the bush
Going back to the question we started with: Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck. The weather that made it possible has become more common, and rising heat is the main reason why. Even the most cautious reading of the evidence puts the increase at 30%, and the researchers themselves think the real number is larger.
It’s also heading one way. At 2°C of global warming, the models suggest seasons like 2019/20 become around eight times more likely than in 1900, and at least four times. That projection rests on just two models, so treat it as a direction rather than a precise prediction.

One thing this study can’t tell you
The Fire Weather Index measures weather, not fire. It says nothing about how much dry fuel is on the ground, what kind of vegetation is near your home, or what starts a fire in the first place. So “fire weather is more likely” doesn’t mean “your house is X% more likely to burn”. It means the days when a fire would be hard to stop are turning up more often.

The practical takeaway is the one fire services have been repeating for years, now with stronger evidence behind it. Seasons that used to feel once-in-a-lifetime should be planned for as something that can happen again. Have a bushfire plan, know your local fire danger rating, and don’t treat a bad summer as a reason to assume the next one will be quieter.

title: The Black Summer wasn’t just bad luck
text:
References


Oldenborgh, G. J. van, F. Krikken, S. Lewis, et al. 2021. “Attribution of the Australian Bushfire Risk to Anthropogenic Climate Change.” Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences 21 (3): 941–60. https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-21-941-2021.

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
text:
For some businesses, forecast accuracy isn’t a nice-to-have. The whole operation rests on it. One bad call can cost a whole season: the prep, the buying, the planning, all built on a number that turned out wrong. So the reliance is huge, which made me wonder how much of it is actually earned.
So I spent a week asking one question about Australian farm forecasts: can you actually trust them?

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
text:
The data
ABARES, the government’s farm economics agency, keeps a record of every forecast it has published since 2000, sitting right next to what actually happened (Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences 2023). That’s more than 22,500 forecasts across 24 commodities, from wheat and cotton to cattle and even the Australian dollar. It’s rare to get data like this, because it lets you score accuracy head-on instead of guessing at it.
I matched it against Bureau of Meteorology rainfall for each financial year to see whether the weather explained the misses. Then I found four things I didn’t expect.

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
section: 1. The further ahead you look, the worse it gets
text:
1. The further ahead you look, the worse it gets






Figure 1: Average forecast error by how many years ahead the forecast was made.



Figure 1 shows it plainly. Forecasts for the current year average about 8.5% error. Push out five years and it climbs to nearly 27%. A forecast is only as good as the assumptions behind it, and the longer you wait, the more time those assumptions have to fall apart.

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
section: 2. “Unbiased” on average isn’t the same as accurate
text:
2. “Unbiased” on average isn’t the same as accurate
At first glance ABARES looks clean. Across everything, its forecasts lean just -1.1%, basically zero. Case closed, you’d think.
Except the average is doing a lot of quiet lying. Break it down by commodity and Whole Milk Powder is forecast 22% too high, cotton 10.5% too high, while maize and lamb come in around 11% too low. Opposite biases wash each other out, so the headline number hides which way each one actually leans.

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
text:
3. Some commodities are just harder






Figure 2: Average forecast error by commodity. Weather-exposed, export-heavy crops sit at the top, shed-raised livestock at the bottom.



Figure 2 is where the spread becomes the whole story. Cotton (37.6%), canola (32.9%) and whole milk powder (30.2%) are the hardest to forecast. Poultry (6.1%), pigs (7.0%) and cattle (9.7%) are the easiest.
The split isn’t random. Cotton and canola live and die by the season’s rainfall and global prices. Poultry and pigs are raised in sheds on planned cycles, barely touched by drought. The more a commodity is at the mercy of weather and world markets, the worse the forecast gets, which matches wider research on volatile commodity markets (zelingher2024?).

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
section: 4. The weather finding almost didn’t exist
text:
4. The weather finding almost didn’t exist
I expected dry years to make the errors bigger. They didn’t. The size of the error barely moved with rainfall, and for a while I thought the whole weather angle was dead.
Then I checked the direction instead (Figure 3).






Figure 3: Average forecast bias in dry, normal and wet years. Positive means the forecast was too high.



In dry years ABARES runs about 20% too high. In wet years it runs about 9% too low. The reason is timing: forecasts are locked in before the season plays out, built on a roughly normal year. A drought sinks the real harvest below the guess. A wet year pushes it past.
One honest limit: this uses national rainfall, one number for the whole continent. It can’t tell a drought in one growing region from a good season in another, which is probably why the direction showed up but the size didn’t.

title: Can you trust Australia’s farm forecasts?
text:
So, can you trust them?
It depends on which one you’re holding. Lean on them for the short term. Treat long-range forecasts for weather-sensitive crops as a starting point, not a promise. The reliance is earned, but only if you know where to put it.
That rainfall pattern is also what got me thinking about climate more broadly, and eventually led to my post on the Black Summer bushfires.
Built in R with tidyverse and Quarto for ETC5512 at Monash. I also shared a shorter version on LinkedIn.

title: About
text:
Hi, I’m Anali.
I studied Banking & Finance and Business Analytics at Monash, and somewhere along the way I noticed the numbers were never the hard part. The hard part was what came after: explaining them to someone who actually had to make a decision. So I came back for a Master of Business Analytics to get better at exactly that.
The more I worked with data, the more I realised the same dataset can mean completely different things depending on who’s holding it. A forecast table that makes sense to an economist means nothing to a farmer watching the sky. A climate study written for scientists doesn’t help the family deciding whether to stay or leave on a bad fire day. I like figuring out how to close that gap.
That’s what this blog is. It started with a question about whether Australia’s farm forecasts can be trusted, and led me to the Black Summer bushfires and what climate change is doing to the places we live.
If you’re here, chances are you care about this stuff too. I try to keep life fun, but I also think our generation needs to stay informed and face what’s actually happening, even when it’s uncomfortable.
Site colours are from Shutterstock’s sustainable design colour palettes, picked to match the climate and farming topics on this blog.
